The West African carp Labeo senegalensis is a commercially important cyprinid distributed throughout the Sahelo-Sudanian river systems, yet its life-history traits remain poorly quantified. Recent field collections in the Niger River basin have provided new data on body size and reproductive parameters. The maximum total length recorded in a sample of over 500 individuals was 65 cm [Li = 65 cm], a value consistent with the upper size range reported for this species in West African inland waters. Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a considerably smaller size; analysis of gonadal development revealed that puberty is attained at a total length of 17.5 cm [Lp = 17.5 cm]. This size at maturity is typical for a medium-bodied cyprinid inhabiting seasonal tropical floodplains, where early maturation is favoured by high adult mortality rates during the dry season. The marked difference between size at puberty and ultimate length underscores a life history strategy that prioritises early reproductive output over extended somatic growth, a pattern observed in many iteroparous teleosts from hydrologically unpredictable environments.

The initial developmental stages of Labeo senegalensis are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of warm, productive floodplain waters. Incubation experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] demonstrated that the eggs hatch after just 4 days [ab = 4 days]. This brief embryonic period is characteristic of tropical cyprinids with small, pelagic eggs that develop rapidly in response to elevated temperatures. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are extremely small; their wet weight at birth was estimated at 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = 0.0005236 grams], a value derived from an assumed egg diameter of one millimetre. This minute birth mass reflects the low maternal investment per offspring, which is compensated for by the production of large numbers of eggs during each spawning event. The larvae remain endotrophic for a short interval, absorbing their yolk reserves before the onset of first exogenous feeding, which typically occurs within the first week post-hatching.

Reproductive output in Labeo senegalensis has been quantified through histological examination of gravid females collected during the peak spawning period in the Niger River. Under the prevailing thermal regime of the floodplain, which averages approximately 24 °C [T = 24 °C], females produce an average clutch size of 293 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 293 eggs per spawning event]. Field studies further indicate that individual females typically complete about one spawning event per year [F_R_i = about one spawning event per year], timed to coincide with the rising water levels of the wet season. This annual bout of reproduction, combined with the moderate fecundity per event, suggests a life history that balances current reproductive investment with the need to survive until the subsequent spawning season. The single annual reproductive bout is typical of many tropical cyprinids that breed in synchrony with the flood pulse, maximising the likelihood of larval survival in newly inundated nursery habitats.

Adult body mass in Labeo senegalensis shows a pronounced increase from the pubertal stage to the fully grown condition. The wet weight at puberty, derived from the length-weight relationship established for this population, is approximately 55.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 55.8 grams]. Individuals continue to gain mass steadily as they mature, with the largest adults attaining an ultimate wet weight of about 3000 grams [Wwi = about 3000 grams]. This massive increase represents a fifty-fold gain in body mass from first reproduction to maximum size, reflecting the continued somatic investment that occurs even after sexual maturation. This pattern is consistent with an indeterminate growth strategy, common among cyprinids, where energy is allocated simultaneously to both reproduction and somatic growth throughout adult life. The heavy adult body mass likely confers advantages in terms of fecundity, as larger females can accommodate greater ovarian volumes, as well as in predator avoidance and competitive dominance within the floodplain fish community.

Longevity and the timing of life cycle events in Labeo senegalensis are strongly influenced by the seasonal thermal regime of its habitat. Maximum lifespan in this species, established from mark-recapture studies and otolith age reading, is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when fish are reared under natural temperature conditions that average around 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This lifespan is relatively short compared to temperate cyprinids of similar body size, a pattern commonly attributed to the high metabolic costs and elevated predation pressure characteristic of tropical freshwater ecosystems. The combination of early maturation at 17.5 cm [Lp = 17.5 cm] total length, a modest lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years], and the production of approximately 293 eggs per annual spawning event [Ri = approximately 293 eggs per annual spawning event] places Labeo senegalensis firmly within the fast-lived end of the cyprinid life-history continuum at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. These demographic parameters have important implications for fisheries management, as the species is heavily exploited throughout its range and may be vulnerable to overfishing if harvest rates exceed its relatively limited reproductive potential.
